common_name: Densa Inkberry Holly (Dense Compact Native Broadleaf Evergreen)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Densa is an older, reliably dense and compact inkberry selection that holds its shape better than many seedling-grown plants.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Densa is a long-established inkberry selection valued for its reliably dense, compact form, holding small, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves on a tighter, fuller shrub than typical seedling-grown inkberry, which tends toward bare, leggy lower growth over time. It serves as a broadleaf evergreen alternative to boxwood, tolerating wetter soil and more shade than boxwood while providing similar year-round structure for a foundation planting or low hedge. Only female plants produce the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator nearby for fruit set. Shear lightly if a more formal shape is wanted, and provide consistently moist, acidic soil.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Compacta Inkberry Holly (Classic Dense Rounded Broadleaf Evergreen)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Compacta is one of the oldest and most widely planted compact inkberry selections, forming a dense rounded mound.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Compacta is one of the oldest and most widely planted compact inkberry cultivars, forming a dense, rounded mound of small, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves that has served for decades as a broadleaf evergreen alternative to boxwood, tolerating wetter soil and more shade than boxwood while providing similar year-round structure. Native to wetlands and pinelands of the eastern and southeastern United States, it can develop bare lower growth with age like other inkberry cultivars, so light annual shearing helps maintain density. Only female plants produce the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator nearby for fruit set.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Nordic Inkberry Holly (Cold-Hardy Compact Dense Broadleaf Evergreen)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Nordic is an exceptionally cold-hardy, dense, compact inkberry selection that holds its rounded form well without shearing.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Nordic bears small, glossy, spineless evergreen leaves on a densely branched, naturally rounded shrub selected for exceptional cold hardiness beyond that of most inkberry cultivars, along with better resistance to the bare, leggy lower growth that plagues older seedling-grown inkberry. It serves as a broadleaf evergreen alternative to boxwood, tolerating wetter soil and more shade than boxwood while providing similar year-round structure for a foundation planting or low hedge. Only female plants produce the small black berries valued by birds, requiring a male pollinator nearby for fruit set.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Bordeaux Yaupon Holly (Dwarf Yaupon with Reddish-Purple Winter Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bordeaux is a dwarf yaupon holly selection whose fine-textured green foliage takes on a reddish-purple tint in cool winter weather.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; yaupon holly tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease. Bordeaux is a compact, dwarf yaupon selection whose small, fine-textured leaves turn an attractive reddish-purple to burgundy tint in cool winter weather, reverting to green as temperatures warm in spring, giving it a seasonal color change most yaupon cultivars lack. Its naturally dense, rounded, low-growing habit makes it useful as a low hedge, foundation planting, or mass groundcover shrub without the shearing needed for taller cultivars. It tolerates both wet and dry soils and is largely indifferent to poor soil and heat, needing minimal maintenance once established.
